title: The OSI model, without the mnemonics
summary: What each layer actually does, and why troubleshooting starts at the bottom.
body:
## The OSI model as a troubleshooting instrument

The mnemonic gets you the order. What the exam actually tests is using the layers to locate a fault — describing a symptom and asking which layer owns it.

### The seven layers, by job

| Layer | Name | Handles | Devices and protocols |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | **Application** | What the user interacts with | HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP |
| 6 | **Presentation** | Formatting, encryption, compression | TLS/SSL, JPEG, ASCII |
| 5 | **Session** | Establishing and tearing down conversations | Session setup, NetBIOS |
| 4 | **Transport** | Reliability, ports, segmentation | TCP, UDP |
| 3 | **Network** | Logical addressing and routing | IP, ICMP, routers |
| 2 | **Data Link** | Local delivery by MAC address | Ethernet, switches, ARP |
| 1 | **Physical** | Bits on the medium | Cables, connectors, signalling |

### Devices by layer

This is asked directly and is worth memorising:

- **Hub, repeater, cable, transceiver** — Layer 1. A hub repeats electrical signals out every port with no idea what they contain.
- **Switch, bridge, NIC, access point** — Layer 2. A switch learns MAC addresses and forwards frames to the correct port.
- **Router, Layer 3 switch, firewall (basic)** — Layer 3. A router forwards by IP address between networks.
- **Load balancer, next-generation firewall, proxy** — Layers 4 through 7, because they make decisions using ports and application content.

A **Layer 3 switch** is the one that trips people: it is a switch that can also route between the VLANs it hosts, using an SVI as each VLAN's gateway. Saying "the switch will not route between VLANs" is only true of a Layer 2 switch.

### Encapsulation, and why the names change

As data descends the stack each layer adds its own header, and the unit gets a different name — which is why the exam uses these terms precisely:

| Layer | Unit |
|---|---|
| Application to Session | **Data** |
| Transport | **Segment** (TCP) or **datagram** (UDP) |
| Network | **Packet** |
| Data Link | **Frame** |
| Physical | **Bits** |

The receiving host reverses the process, stripping each header on the way up. So a "frame" is a Layer 2 concept and a "packet" is Layer 3 — if a question mentions frames, it is talking about the switching layer.

### Using layers to troubleshoot

The practical value is narrowing. Ask: **what is the lowest layer that could explain this?**

| Symptom | Likely layer |
|---|---|
| No link light at all | 1 — cable, port, transceiver |
| Link up, but two devices on the same switch cannot talk | 2 — VLAN assignment, MAC issues |
| Same-subnet works, different-subnet does not | 3 — routing, gateway, subnet mask |
| Host reachable but one service refuses connections | 4 — port blocked or not listening |
| The application errors while everything else works | 7 — the application or its configuration |

A fault at a low layer explains every failure above it, which is why **bottom-up** is usually the efficient direction: confirm the physical link before theorising about DNS.

**Divide and conquer** is the alternative named approach — test at the middle of the stack, and whichever half proves faulty gets divided again. It is faster when you have a strong hypothesis about roughly where the problem sits.

### TCP/IP model mapping

The four-layer TCP/IP model is what the internet actually runs on, and the exam sometimes maps between them:

| TCP/IP layer | OSI equivalent |
|---|---|
| Application | 5, 6, 7 |
| Transport | 4 |
| Internet | 3 |
| Network Access / Link | 1 and 2 |

> Exam habit: when a scenario says a device "has a valid IP address and can ping its gateway," Layers 1 through 3 are working. The fault is at Layer 4 or above — a blocked port, a stopped service, or name resolution.

title: Subnetting: the only two numbers you actually need
summary: How to go from a CIDR prefix to usable hosts without a cheat sheet.
body:
## Subnetting: two facts and some arithmetic

Subnetting panics people because it looks like maths. It is really two facts plus counting.

### Fact 1: the prefix tells you the host bits

An IPv4 address is 32 bits. A **/24** means 24 bits identify the network, leaving **8 bits for hosts**:

**Total addresses = 2 raised to the number of host bits**

| Prefix | Host bits | Total addresses |
|---|---|---|
| /24 | 8 | 256 |
| /25 | 7 | 128 |
| /26 | 6 | 64 |
| /27 | 5 | 32 |
| /28 | 4 | 16 |
| /29 | 3 | 8 |
| /30 | 2 | 4 |

### Fact 2: subtract two for usable hosts

Every subnet reserves its **first** address as the network identifier and its **last** as the broadcast address:

**Usable hosts = 2^(host bits) − 2**

| Prefix | Total | Usable |
|---|---|---|
| /24 | 256 | 254 |
| /26 | 64 | 62 |
| /28 | 16 | 14 |
| /30 | 4 | **2** |

A **/30** giving exactly two usable addresses is why point-to-point router links traditionally use it — one address for each end and nothing wasted.

### The exam's favourite question

> "You need 100 usable hosts on one subnet. What is the smallest prefix that fits?"

Work backwards from the host count. You need 2^n − 2 ≥ 100:

- n = 6 gives 62. Not enough.
- n = 7 gives 126. Enough.

Seven host bits means the prefix is 32 − 7 = **/25**. No chart required.

### Reading the mask

Each octet of a subnet mask is the binary value of its bits:

| Mask octet | Binary | Bits |
|---|---|---|
| 255 | 11111111 | 8 |
| 254 | 11111110 | 7 |
| 252 | 11111100 | 6 |
| 248 | 11111000 | 5 |
| 240 | 11110000 | 4 |
| 224 | 11100000 | 3 |
| 192 | 11000000 | 2 |
| 128 | 10000000 | 1 |

So 255.255.255.192 is 8 + 8 + 8 + 2 = **/26**.

### Finding which subnet an address belongs to

The **block size** is 256 minus the interesting octet of the mask. For a /26, the mask octet is 192, so the block size is 64 — subnets start at 0, 64, 128, and 192.

An address of 192.168.1.100/26 therefore falls in the 64–127 block:

- Network address: 192.168.1.64
- First usable: 192.168.1.65
- Last usable: 192.168.1.126
- Broadcast: 192.168.1.127

That block-size method answers most "which subnet / what is the broadcast address" questions quickly.

### VLSM and CIDR

**CIDR** (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) abandoned the old rigid class boundaries, so any prefix length may be used and routes can be summarised.

**VLSM** (Variable Length Subnet Mask) takes it further: different subnets within the same network can use different prefix lengths, sized to their actual need. A 200-host user network gets a /24 while a router-to-router link gets a /30, instead of wasting a /24 on two addresses. This is standard practice and the reason address space stretches as far as it does.

### IPv4 address classes

Pre-CIDR, addresses were divided by leading bits. Still tested:

| Class | First octet | Default mask | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1–126 | /8 | Very large networks |
| B | 128–191 | /16 | Medium networks |
| C | 192–223 | /24 | Small networks |
| D | 224–239 | — | Multicast |
| E | 240–255 | — | Experimental |

127 is reserved for **loopback**, which is why it is missing from the Class A range in practice.

> Exam habit: the two formulas are 2^n for total addresses and 2^n − 2 for usable hosts. Almost every subnetting question is one of those two, run forwards or backwards.

title: DNS record types and what each one resolves
summary: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, and the rest — matched to the question that names them.
body:
## DNS: record types, resolution, and where it breaks

DNS turns names into addresses, and the exam tests both the record types and how a lookup actually proceeds.

### The record types

| Record | Maps | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Hostname to IPv4 address | The most common record |
| **AAAA** | Hostname to IPv6 address | "Quad A" |
| **CNAME** | Alias to another name | Points to a name, never to an address |
| **MX** | Domain to its mail servers | Includes a priority value |
| **TXT** | Arbitrary text | Carries SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and domain-ownership proofs |
| **NS** | Domain to its authoritative name servers | Delegation |
| **PTR** | IP address back to a name | Reverse lookup |
| **SOA** | Start of Authority | Zone metadata: primary server, serial, timers |
| **SRV** | Service location | Used heavily by Active Directory and SIP |

Two distinctions get tested. **CNAME points to a name, A points to an address** — so a CNAME whose target does not resolve produces a failure one step removed from where you are looking. And **TXT records are where email authentication lives**: SPF lists which servers may send for the domain, DKIM publishes the signing key, and DMARC states what to do when the first two fail.

### How a recursive lookup works

When a client asks for `www.example.com` and nothing is cached:

1. The client asks its configured **recursive resolver**.
2. The resolver asks a **root** server, which points to the **.com** TLD servers.
3. The TLD servers point to the **authoritative** name servers for `example.com`.
4. Those authoritative servers return the actual record.
5. The resolver caches the answer for its **TTL** and returns it to the client.

The client made one **recursive** query; the resolver made several **iterative** ones on its behalf. That is the distinction behind the terms.

### Authoritative versus non-authoritative

An **authoritative** answer comes from a server that actually holds the zone. A **non-authoritative** answer comes from a resolver's cache. `nslookup` labels its output accordingly, and "non-authoritative answer" is normal — not an error.

### Zones and server roles

- **Forward zone** — names to addresses. The everyday direction.
- **Reverse zone** — addresses to names, using PTR records. Mail servers check these as an anti-spam signal.
- **Primary** — holds the writable copy of the zone.
- **Secondary** — holds a read-only replica, transferred from the primary, providing redundancy and load sharing.

### TTL and caching

Every record carries a **TTL** telling resolvers how long they may cache it. This is the reason DNS changes are not instant: until the old TTL expires, resolvers everywhere keep serving the previous answer.

The practical consequence is a planning step: **lower the TTL well before a planned migration**, so the cutover propagates quickly, then raise it again afterwards. A record with a 24-hour TTL changed at the moment of migration means a day of inconsistent results.

Locally, `ipconfig /flushdns` clears the client's cache, which is the fix for a workstation still using a stale record after a change.

### Securing and hardening DNS

- **DNSSEC** signs records so a resolver can verify they were not tampered with in transit. It provides authenticity, **not** confidentiality — the queries are still readable.
- **DNS over HTTPS (DoH)** and **DNS over TLS (DoT)** encrypt the query itself, protecting privacy against an observer on the network.
- **Internal versus external (split-horizon) DNS** returns different answers depending on where the query came from, so internal hostnames are not published to the world.

### Common failures

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| `ping 8.8.8.8` works, `ping google.com` does not | DNS resolution is broken; connectivity is fine |
| Site resolves to the wrong address | Stale cache, or **DNS poisoning** |
| Change made but old address still returned | TTL has not expired |
| Some clients work, others do not | Clients using different resolvers |
| Domain-joined machines fail authentication | Clients pointing at a public resolver instead of the domain controllers |

That last row is a real-world classic worth carrying: domain members **must** use the internal DNS servers, because that is where the SRV records locating domain controllers live. Pointing a domain workstation at 8.8.8.8 breaks logon in ways that look nothing like a DNS problem.

**The hosts file** is checked before DNS is consulted at all, which makes it both a useful testing tool and a favourite malware target for silently redirecting traffic.

> Exam habit: substituting an IP address for a hostname is the single fastest way to prove whether a fault is DNS. If the IP works and the name does not, stop looking at cables.

title: Appliances, cloud service models, and the physical-layer odds and ends
summary: What each network appliance does, IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, address classes, traffic types, and the connectors/media you're expected to name.
body:
## Naming the boxes and the bits that don't get their own lesson

### Network appliances, by job

- **Load balancer** — spreads client requests across multiple servers, so no single server is overwhelmed and one server failing doesn't take the service down.
- **Proxy** — sits between clients and destinations, making requests on clients' behalf (caching, content filtering, hiding internal addresses).
- **NAS (Network Attached Storage)** — file-level storage accessed over the network (think a shared drive) — simple to set up, good for general file sharing.
- **SAN (Storage Area Network)** — block-level storage that appears to servers as if it were a local disk — higher performance, used for databases and virtualization back-ends.
- **IDS vs IPS** — an **IDS** (Intrusion Detection System) monitors and alerts on suspicious traffic; an **IPS** (Intrusion Prevention System) sits inline and can actively block it. Detection vs. prevention is the whole distinction.

> Exam habit: "file share for general documents" → NAS. "Storage backend for a database or VM cluster, needs to look like a local disk" → SAN.

### An application and two functions worth naming

- **CDN (Content Delivery Network)** — caches content on servers geographically close to users, so a video or web asset loads from a nearby edge node instead of crossing the whole internet to the origin server every time.
- **QoS (Quality of Service)** — prioritizes some traffic over others on a congested link, so latency-sensitive traffic like VoIP doesn't get stuck behind a large file transfer.
- **TTL (Time to Live)** — a counter on every IP packet that decrements at each router hop; when it hits zero the packet is discarded. It exists to stop a misrouted packet from looping forever, and it's also what `traceroute` manipulates to map a path hop by hop.

### Cloud gateways and the constructs inside a VPC

Inside a cloud provider's virtual private cloud, a few named pieces do specific jobs:

- **Internet gateway** — the VPC's attachment point to the public internet; a subnet without a route to one is effectively private, no matter how its security rules are set.
- **NAT gateway** — lets instances in a private subnet initiate outbound internet connections (for updates, API calls) without being directly reachable from the internet themselves — the cloud version of the NAT your home router does.
- **Network security groups** and **network security lists** — both are firewall-like rule sets controlling traffic to cloud resources, but they work at different scopes: a security group is typically attached to an instance/interface (stateful, allow-rules only in many providers), while a security list/network ACL applies at the subnet level and can be stateless with explicit deny rules — layering both is a common design.

### GRE and IPSec, as IP protocol types

- **GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation)** — wraps one packet inside another so traffic that wouldn't normally survive a path (a different protocol, a routing requirement) can tunnel across it. GRE by itself adds no encryption — it's a tunneling mechanism, not a security one.
- **IPSec (Internet Protocol Security)** — the protocol suite that actually secures VPN traffic, built from three named pieces:
  - **AH (Authentication Header)** — authenticates the packet and guarantees integrity, but doesn't encrypt the payload.
  - **ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload)** — encrypts the payload (and can also authenticate it) — this is the piece doing the actual confidentiality work.
  - **IKE (Internet Key Exchange)** — negotiates and manages the encryption keys both ends use, before AH/ESP ever move data.

> Exam habit: GRE tunnels; IPSec secures. A GRE tunnel is often wrapped *inside* IPSec specifically because GRE alone provides no encryption.

### Cloud service models

- **IaaS** — you get virtual hardware (compute/storage/network); you manage the OS up.
- **PaaS** — you get a platform to deploy code onto; the provider manages the OS and runtime.
- **SaaS** — you get finished software; the provider manages everything.

Each step up hands more of the stack to the provider — same idea whether it's Network+ or A+ testing it.

### IPv4 address classes

Before CIDR, addresses were divided into classes by their leading bits — mostly historical now, but still tested:

| Class | First octet range | Default mask | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1–126 | /8 | Very large networks |
| B | 128–191 | /16 | Medium networks |
| C | 192–223 | /24 | Small networks |
| D | 224–239 | — | Multicast |
| E | 240–255 | — | Experimental/reserved |

(127 is reserved for loopback and doesn't belong to Class A in practice, even though it falls in that numeric range.)

### Traffic types

- **Unicast** — one sender to one specific receiver. Most traffic.
- **Broadcast** — one sender to *every* device on the local segment (the broadcast address at the top of a subnet).
- **Multicast** — one sender to a specific *group* of interested receivers (streaming to subscribers, routing protocol updates) — not everyone, not just one.
- **Anycast** — one address that routes to the *nearest* of several servers advertising it — used by things like public DNS resolvers, where "nearest" gives the best performance.

### Connectors and media you're expected to recognize

| Connector/media | Used for |
|---|---|
| **SC, LC, ST** | Fiber connectors — LC is the small modern one common in datacenters, ST is the older twist-lock/bayonet style |
| **MPO** | A single connector carrying multiple fiber strands at once — high-density fiber runs |
| **RJ11** | Telephone-style jack — smaller than RJ45, used for phone lines/older DSL |
| **F-type** | Coaxial cable connector — cable internet/TV |
| **BNC** | Older coaxial connector, twist-lock — legacy Ethernet and some video/lab equipment |
| **Coaxial** | Single conductor with shielding — cable internet, legacy 10BASE2 Ethernet |
| **DAC (Direct Attach Copper)** | A fixed copper cable with transceivers built onto both ends — short high-speed runs between adjacent switches, cheaper than fiber+optics over short distances |
| **Satellite / cellular** | Wireless WAN media for locations without wired options, or as a backup link |

### Plenum cable, and a transceiver protocol besides Ethernet

**Plenum-rated cable** has a jacket that doesn't release toxic fumes when it burns, required by fire code for runs through a plenum space — the area above a drop ceiling or under a raised floor that also carries building air. Regular **PVC-jacketed cable** is cheaper but code-illegal in those spaces; running standard cable through a plenum is a fire-code violation, not just a suboptimal choice.

Most transceivers you'll deal with speak **Ethernet**, but SAN environments often use **Fibre Channel (FC)** instead — a protocol purpose-built for high-speed, low-latency storage traffic between servers and a SAN, distinct from the IP-based Ethernet stack everything else on the exam assumes.

### Topologies you'll see as distractors turned real answers

- **Three-tier** — the classic core/distribution/access layered design.
- **Collapsed core** — a smaller network merges the core and distribution layers into one tier, since a small deployment doesn't need three separate layers of switching.

title: Evolving network environments: SDN's cousins, Zero Trust, SASE, and Infrastructure as Code
summary: VXLAN, ZTA's control/data plane split, SASE/SSE, and treating network config like source code.
body:
## Evolving network environments

The newer vocabulary the exam expects you to recognise, and the problem each thing was invented to solve.

### SDN and SD-WAN

**Software-defined networking** separates the **control plane** (deciding where traffic should go) from the **data plane** (actually forwarding it). Traditionally every switch and router made its own decisions locally. SDN centralises those decisions in a controller, so policy is defined once and pushed out, and the network becomes programmable rather than device-by-device.

**SD-WAN** applies the idea to wide-area links. Its named characteristics:

- **Application aware** — recognises traffic types and steers them by policy, so voice takes the low-latency path while backups take the cheap one.
- **Zero-touch provisioning** — a new branch device fetches its configuration automatically on first boot, without an engineer on site.
- **Transport agnostic** — treats MPLS, broadband, and cellular as interchangeable underlying links.
- **Central policy management** — one place to define behaviour for every site.

### VXLAN

A standard 802.1Q VLAN ID is 12 bits, giving about 4,094 usable VLANs — not enough for a large multi-tenant data centre.

**VXLAN** wraps the original Layer 2 frame inside a UDP packet with a **24-bit identifier**, supporting over 16 million logical segments. Because the result is a routable UDP packet, that Layer 2 segment can be carried across a Layer 3 backbone — which is what enables **DCI** (Data Center Interconnect), stretching a Layer 2 network between sites so a virtual machine can move without changing its IP address.

### Zero Trust Architecture

**ZTA** replaces the old model — trust everything inside the perimeter, distrust everything outside — with continuous verification of every request regardless of origin. The reasoning is that a perimeter is meaningless once an attacker is inside it, or once the workforce is remote.

CompTIA splits it into two planes:

| Plane | Contains | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Control plane** | Policy engine, policy administrator, adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, policy-driven access control | **Decides** |
| **Data plane** | Policy enforcement point, implicit trust zones, subject/system | **Enforces** |

- **Adaptive identity** — trust adjusts with context (device posture, location, behaviour), not just a successful login.
- **Threat scope reduction** — deliberately narrowing what any single identity can reach, so a compromised credential yields the smallest possible blast radius.
- **Least privilege access** — the same principle applied to permissions.

The short version: the control plane makes the decision, the data plane applies it.

### SASE and SSE

**SASE** (Secure Access Service Edge) converges networking (SD-WAN) with cloud-delivered security — firewall, secure web gateway, zero-trust access, CASB — into a single service at the edge. A remote user or branch gets both connectivity and security from the nearest point of presence, instead of backhauling all traffic to a data centre for inspection first.

**SSE** (Security Service Edge) is the security-only subset: SASE without the SD-WAN half.

### Infrastructure as Code

**IaC** treats network configuration the way software teams treat source code.

**Automation:**

- **Playbooks, templates, and reusable tasks** define configuration once and apply it repeatedly and identically.
- **Configuration drift and compliance** — devices are checked against their intended state, and deviations corrected.
- **Upgrades** are applied consistently across a fleet rather than device by device.
- **Dynamic inventories** track what actually exists, so automation targets the right set as the estate changes.

**Source control:**

- **Version control** records every change and who made it.
- A **central repository** is the single source of truth.
- **Conflict identification** catches two people editing the same configuration.
- **Branching** lets a change be developed and tested in isolation before merging.

The payoff is that a network change goes through the same review-and-rollback discipline as a code change, instead of being a manual edit nobody else can see or revert.

### IPv6 adoption

IPv6's 128-bit addresses exist to **mitigate address exhaustion** — the reason NAT became universal in IPv4. Compatibility mechanisms:

- **Dual stack** — run both protocols at once. The most common approach.
- **Tunneling** — carry IPv6 across an IPv4-only path.
- **NAT64** — translate between IPv6-only clients and IPv4-only servers.

> Exam habit: each term answers one problem. VXLAN answers VLAN exhaustion at cloud scale. ZTA answers the failure of perimeter trust. SASE answers backhauling remote traffic for inspection. IaC answers inconsistent manual configuration. Matching the problem to the term is the whole question.

title: VLANs and trunking: why segmentation exists
summary: Access vs trunk ports, and what 802.1Q tagging actually does.
body:
## VLANs and trunking: why segmentation exists

A **VLAN** splits one physical switch into several logical networks. Devices in different VLANs cannot reach each other without a router, and that is precisely the point.

### What a VLAN buys you

- **Broadcast containment.** Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain, so broadcast traffic does not cross the whole site.
- **Security separation.** Guest Wi-Fi, IoT devices, and the finance department can share physical switches while remaining logically apart.
- **Logical grouping regardless of location.** Users on three floors can sit in one VLAN without recabling.
- **Simpler policy.** Firewall rules between VLANs are far easier to express than per-device rules.

### Access ports and trunk ports

- An **access port** belongs to exactly one VLAN and carries untagged traffic. End devices plug into these and have no idea VLANs exist.
- A **trunk port** carries several VLANs over one link, using **802.1Q** tagging to label which VLAN each frame belongs to. Switch-to-switch links and router-on-a-stick connections are trunks.

**802.1Q** inserts a 4-byte tag between the source MAC and the EtherType field, containing a 12-bit VLAN ID — which is where the ceiling of 4,094 usable VLANs comes from, and why VXLAN exists for larger environments.

### The native VLAN

The **native VLAN** is the one VLAN on a trunk sent **untagged**, for backward compatibility. Two things about it are tested:

- A **native VLAN mismatch** between the two ends of a trunk merges traffic between two different VLANs — a genuine security problem, and one that often produces confusing partial connectivity.
- Leaving the native VLAN as the default VLAN 1 enables **double-tagging VLAN hopping**. Best practice is to set the native VLAN to an unused ID carrying no user traffic.

### Voice VLAN

A dedicated VLAN for VoIP traffic, kept separate so voice receives consistent QoS treatment instead of competing with file transfers. A desk phone with a PC plugged into its pass-through port typically tags its own traffic onto the voice VLAN while the PC's traffic stays untagged on the data VLAN — one cable, one switch port, two VLANs.

### Inter-VLAN routing

VLANs need a Layer 3 device to talk to each other. Two designs:

- **Router on a stick** — one physical router interface carries a trunk, with a **subinterface** per VLAN acting as that VLAN's gateway. Simple, but all inter-VLAN traffic crosses one link.
- **Layer 3 switch with SVIs** — a **switch virtual interface** is configured per VLAN with an IP address, and the switch routes between them internally at hardware speed. This is the normal modern design.

An **SVI** is therefore just "the VLAN's gateway, living inside the switch."

### Other interface configuration

- **Link aggregation** (LACP, 802.3ad) bundles several physical links into one logical link for more bandwidth and redundancy. Both ends must be configured to match.
- **Speed and duplex** should normally be left to auto-negotiation on both ends. Hard-setting one side and auto-negotiating the other causes a **duplex mismatch**: the link works but collapses under load.
- **MTU and jumbo frames** — frames larger than the standard 1500 bytes reduce per-packet overhead on storage and backup networks. Every device along the path must agree, or frames are fragmented or dropped.

### Spanning tree

Redundant switch links create loops, and a Layer 2 loop is catastrophic — broadcasts circulate forever and saturate the network within seconds, because Ethernet frames have no TTL to expire them.

**STP** (and the faster **RSTP**) prevents this by electing a **root bridge** and blocking redundant paths, bringing them into service automatically if the active path fails. Related features:

- **PortFast** moves an access port straight to forwarding, since an end device cannot create a loop.
- **BPDU guard** shuts a PortFast port down if it receives a BPDU — meaning someone plugged a switch into an access port. This is a common cause of an **err-disabled** port.

### Troubleshooting VLAN problems

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Device has link but reaches nothing | Access port in the wrong VLAN |
| Only one VLAN crosses a switch-to-switch link | Port is access when it should be trunk |
| Some VLANs cross a trunk, others do not | Allowed VLAN list on the trunk |
| Odd traffic leakage between two VLANs | Native VLAN mismatch |
| Network saturates and devices become unreachable | Layer 2 loop; check STP |

> Exam habit: a device with a perfect cable, a link light, and no connectivity at all is very often an access port assigned to the wrong VLAN. Layer 1 is fine; Layer 2 segmentation is doing exactly what it was told.

title: Wireless standards and the 2.4 vs 5 GHz trade-off
summary: 802.11 generations, and why the exam keeps asking about range vs speed.
body:
## Wireless: bands, channels, and the settings that matter

Most wireless questions come down to a trade between range and capacity, or to naming a setting from its effect.

### The bands

| Band | Range | Channels | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **2.4 GHz** | Longest | Only **3** non-overlapping (1, 6, 11) | Penetrates walls well; heavily congested |
| **5 GHz** | Shorter | Many non-overlapping | Faster, cleaner, less wall penetration |
| **6 GHz** | Shortest | Most spectrum available | Wi-Fi 6E and later; cleanest but least reach |

The 2.4 GHz band is crowded not only with Wi-Fi but with Bluetooth, microwaves, and cordless phones. Its three non-overlapping channels are why dense deployments struggle there.

**Reading the symptom** is the exam skill:

- Weak signal far from the AP, no congestion — a **coverage** problem. More APs or better placement; 2.4 GHz reaches further.
- Full signal, poor throughput at busy times — a **capacity/contention** problem. Separate channels properly and steer clients to 5 or 6 GHz.

Raising transmit power is the tempting wrong answer for the second case: it enlarges the interference footprint and usually makes dense-deployment contention worse.

### Channel width

Wider channels (40, 80, 160 MHz) carry more data per transmission but consume more spectrum, leaving fewer non-overlapping channels. On 2.4 GHz, where there are only three to begin with, wide channels are almost always counterproductive.

### The generations

| Standard | Name | Bands | Notable |
|---|---|---|---|
| 802.11n | Wi-Fi 4 | 2.4 and 5 | Introduced MIMO |
| 802.11ac | Wi-Fi 5 | 5 only | MU-MIMO, higher throughput |
| 802.11ax | Wi-Fi 6 / 6E | 2.4, 5, (6E adds 6) | OFDMA; much better in dense environments |

You will not be asked to recite data rates. You will be asked which band or generation solves a described symptom.

### Naming an access point

- **SSID** — the network name users select.
- **BSSID** — one specific AP radio's MAC address. A multi-AP network has many BSSIDs.
- **ESSID** — the shared name presented across all of them, which is what makes roaming feel seamless.

**Band steering** nudges dual-band-capable clients onto 5 or 6 GHz rather than letting them default to the crowded 2.4 GHz band.

**802.11h** is a regulatory amendment requiring **dynamic frequency selection** and transmit power control on 5 GHz channels that overlap weather and military radar, so the network yields those channels when radar is detected.

### Encryption and authentication

| Standard | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **WEP** | Broken; recoverable in minutes. Never deploy. |
| **WPA** | Deprecated; TKIP was a stopgap. |
| **WPA2** | AES-CCMP. Still acceptable. |
| **WPA3** | Current best; SAE handshake resists offline dictionary attacks. |

The authentication split matters more than the cipher for exam purposes:

- **PSK (Personal)** — one shared passphrase for everyone. Simple, but there is no per-user accountability, and a leak requires changing it for all users.
- **Enterprise** — 802.1X against a RADIUS server, issuing individual credentials. One person's access can be revoked without touching anyone else.

Any scenario requiring per-user revocation or accountability needs **Enterprise**.

### Network types and topologies

- **Infrastructure** — clients associate with an access point. The normal mode.
- **Ad hoc** — devices connect directly with no AP.
- **Mesh** — nodes relay for each other, extending coverage without cabling every node.
- **Point to point** — a directional link bridging two locations.

### Antennas

**Omnidirectional** antennas radiate evenly in all directions, suiting a centrally placed AP in an open area. **Directional** antennas (Yagi, panel) concentrate energy along one axis, suiting long corridors and point-to-point links.

The classic scenario: an AP with an omnidirectional antenna covering a long hallway wastes most of its energy into the walls. A directional antenna aimed down the hall fixes it.

### Guest access

A **guest network** is a separate SSID isolated from internal resources, giving visitors internet without a path to file shares. A **captive portal** intercepts the first web request and requires login, acceptance of terms, or payment before granting access.

### Autonomous versus lightweight APs

An **autonomous** AP is configured individually and makes its own decisions. A **lightweight** AP is managed by a central **wireless LAN controller** that pushes configuration and coordinates channels, power, and roaming. Beyond a handful of APs, controller-based management is the only practical approach.

### Wireless troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Poor throughput, strong signal | Channel overlap, co-channel interference |
| Signal drops at range | Insufficient coverage; attenuation through walls |
| Clients disconnect while moving | Roaming misconfiguration; overlapping cells too small |
| Intermittent interference | Non-Wi-Fi sources on 2.4 GHz |
| Clients attach to the wrong AP | Sticky clients; band steering or power tuning needed |

A **site survey** and **heat map** document actual coverage and are how AP placement is planned rather than guessed.

> Exam habit: full bars with poor speed is contention, not coverage — and the fix is channel planning or band steering, never turning the power up.

title: More routing protocols, and getting the physical install right
summary: BGP and EIGRP alongside OSPF, jumbo frames, VIPs, and the power/environmental basics.
body:
## Routing: how a router chooses, and what it does with addresses

Routing questions are usually one of two things: which route wins, or which protocol suits the situation.

### Static versus dynamic

**Static routes** are configured by hand. Predictable and zero overhead, but they do not adapt — if the path fails, traffic keeps being sent at it until someone intervenes. Appropriate for small networks, stub sites, and default routes.

**Dynamic routing protocols** exchange information between routers and adapt automatically to changes. They cost some CPU and bandwidth and buy resilience.

### The protocols

| Protocol | Type | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| **OSPF** | Link-state | Interior — within one organisation |
| **EIGRP** | Advanced distance-vector | Interior — Cisco-originated |
| **BGP** | Path-vector | **Exterior** — between organisations and ISPs |

The distinction the exam draws: **inside** one organisation is OSPF or EIGRP; **between** organisations or with an ISP is BGP. BGP is what actually runs the internet, exchanging routes between autonomous systems, and it makes decisions on policy and path attributes rather than purely on speed.

### Route selection, in order

When a router has more than one way to reach a destination, it decides in this order:

1. **Longest prefix match.** The most specific route always wins. A /24 beats a /16 for an address inside it, regardless of protocol or metric — this is checked first and settles most cases.
2. **Administrative distance.** Among routes of equal prefix length from *different* sources, the lowest AD wins. It is a trust rating: directly connected is 0, static is 1, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120.
3. **Metric.** Among routes from the *same* protocol, the protocol's own cost decides — OSPF uses bandwidth-derived cost, RIP uses hop count.

That order is exam material. A static route (AD 1) beats an OSPF route (AD 110) for the same prefix — but a more specific OSPF route beats a less specific static one, because prefix length is evaluated first.

### Address translation

**NAT** rewrites private source addresses to a public one so an internal network can reach the internet. **PAT** (also called NAT overload) extends this by also tracking **port numbers**, which is what lets hundreds of internal hosts share a single public address — the router distinguishes sessions by port.

Almost every home and small-office router performs PAT, even though people usually say "NAT."

### First hop redundancy

Hosts point at a single default gateway address. If that router fails, everything stops. **FHRP** — VRRP, HSRP, or GLBP — lets two or more routers share a **virtual IP** that hosts use as their gateway. One router is active; if it fails, another takes over the VIP. Hosts change nothing and notice nothing.

### Subinterfaces

A single physical router interface can be divided into **subinterfaces**, each carrying one VLAN and acting as that VLAN's gateway. This is the "router on a stick" design: one trunked link to the switch, one subinterface per VLAN.

### Physical installation factors

Getting equipment installed correctly is examined alongside the logical configuration:

**Locations.** The **MDF** (main distribution frame) is the primary point where external circuits and the core equipment live; **IDFs** (intermediate distribution frames) are the wiring closets serving floors or areas, connected back to the MDF.

**Racks and airflow.** Rack space is measured in **rack units**. Equipment must be oriented for **port-side exhaust or intake** consistently, so hot exhaust from one device does not feed the intake of the next. Cabinets should be **lockable**.

**Cabling.** **Patch panels** terminate permanent cable runs, with short patch cords connecting them to switch ports — so the permanent cable is never repeatedly flexed. **Fiber distribution panels** do the same for fiber.

**Power.**

| Item | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **UPS** | Battery runtime through short outages; allows clean shutdown |
| **PDU** | Distributes power within the rack, often with per-outlet monitoring |
| **Power load** | The total draw must stay within circuit and UPS capacity |
| **Voltage** | Equipment must match the supply, and be properly grounded |

**Environmental factors.** Network equipment generates real heat at scale, so cooling and airflow matter. **Humidity** must be controlled in both directions — too dry increases static, too humid risks condensation and corrosion. **Fire suppression** in equipment spaces should be a clean agent rather than water.

A switch that reboots randomly in an unventilated closet each summer afternoon is an **environmental** problem, not a faulty switch — check the room before replacing hardware.

> Exam habit: for route selection, check prefix length first, then administrative distance, then metric. Most "which route is used" questions are settled at step one.

title: Monitoring: SNMP, NetFlow, and knowing which one to reach for
summary: The difference between polling, traps, and flow data.
body:
## Monitoring: choosing the right instrument

Three technologies answer three different questions. Picking the wrong one is the mistake the exam tests.

### SNMP: device health and status

**SNMP** (Simple Network Management Protocol) lets a monitoring station read values from network devices — interface counters, CPU, memory, temperature, uptime.

It works two ways:

- **Polling** — the manager asks each device at intervals. Predictable, but a failure is only noticed at the next poll.
- **Traps** — the device pushes an alert the instant a defined event occurs. Much faster to notice a problem, and the answer whenever a question describes immediate notification.

Supporting concepts:

- **MIB** (Management Information Base) — the structured catalogue of what values a device exposes.
- **OID** — the specific numeric identifier of one value within the MIB.
- **Community strings** — the shared secret in v1 and v2c, sent in **cleartext**. Default strings like `public` and `private` are effectively no security at all.
- **SNMPv3** adds per-user authentication and optional encryption, which is why it is the version to deploy.

### Flow data: who is talking to whom

**NetFlow** and its relatives summarise *conversations* — source, destination, ports, protocol, byte and packet counts — without storing the contents.

This is how you answer "which host is consuming the WAN link" or "what is this server talking to." It scales to a whole network because it stores metadata rather than payload.

### Packet capture: the actual bytes

A **protocol analyser** such as Wireshark captures full packet contents, letting you inspect exactly what was sent. It is the only tool that answers "what was actually in the traffic," and it is essential for protocol-level faults — a failing handshake, a malformed response, a retransmission storm.

The cost is volume. Capturing everything on a busy link produces enormous files quickly, which is precisely why flow data exists for the broader question.

### Choosing between them

| Question | Tool |
|---|---|
| Is this device up, and how loaded is it? | SNMP |
| Which hosts are using the bandwidth? | Flow data |
| What exactly is inside this conversation? | Packet capture |
| What happened, across many devices, in order? | Syslog and SIEM |

### Getting traffic to the analyser

A switch forwards frames only to the destination port, so a sniffer plugged into an ordinary port sees very little. Two solutions:

- **Port mirroring (SPAN)** — the switch copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. Software-configured and convenient, but the switch may drop mirrored frames under load.
- **Network tap** — a hardware device inserted into the link that passively copies traffic. More reliable and does not burden the switch, but requires physically breaking the link to install.

### Logging and log aggregation

**Syslog** is the standard for devices to send log messages to a central collector. Centralising matters for two reasons: correlating events across devices, and integrity — an attacker who compromises a device can clear its local log but not the copy already shipped elsewhere.

A **SIEM** goes further, aggregating and correlating logs to surface patterns no single device would reveal.

Syslog messages carry a **severity level** from 0 (emergency) to 7 (debug), which is how you filter noise from significant events.

### Baselines and alerting

A **baseline** records what normal looks like — typical utilisation, latency, error rates. Its entire value is comparison: "the link is at 60%" is meaningless without knowing that it normally runs at 20%. **Anomaly alerting** fires when current values deviate from that baseline.

Note the distinction from a **configuration baseline**, which is the known-good device configuration used to detect drift. One describes traffic, the other describes settings.

### Other named methods

- **API integration** — modern platforms pull telemetry from cloud services that expose no SNMP.
- **Network discovery** — scheduled or ad hoc scanning to find what is actually on the network.
- **Performance, availability, and configuration monitoring** — the three broad categories the objectives name.

> Exam habit: SNMP for device health, flow data for traffic patterns, packet capture for exact contents. Match the tool to what the question is genuinely asking, not to whichever is most powerful.

title: High availability and the documents that define it
summary: Active-active vs active-passive, and SLA/MOU/NDA in plain terms.
body:
## High availability, disaster recovery, and the documents that define them

Two related questions: how do you keep a service running, and how do you get it back when it stops.

### Redundancy designs

- **Active-active** — all nodes handle traffic simultaneously. Better resource use, and losing one leaves capacity running, though the survivors must be able to absorb the load.
- **Active-passive** — one node works while a standby waits. Simpler and more predictable, but the standby's capacity is idle until needed.

The exam's follow-up is usually about **capacity planning**: redundancy that cannot actually carry the load after a failure is not redundancy. Two servers each running at 70% cannot absorb each other.

### Redundancy at each layer

| Layer | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Power | UPS for short outages, generator for extended ones, dual PSUs per device |
| Network path | Multiple links, **link aggregation**, spanning tree for loop-free redundancy |
| Default gateway | **FHRP** — VRRP or HSRP — presenting a shared **VIP** so failover is invisible to hosts |
| Server | Clustering, load balancing |
| Storage | RAID, replication |
| Site | Hot, warm, or cold standby sites |

**FHRP** is the one worth understanding. Hosts point at a single default gateway address; if that router dies, everything stops. A first hop redundancy protocol lets two routers share a **virtual IP**, with one active and the other ready. Hosts never change their configuration and never notice the switch.

### DR metrics

| Metric | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective) | How much data can we afford to lose, measured in time? |
| **RTO** (Recovery Time Objective) | How quickly must service be restored? |
| **MTTR** (Mean Time To Repair) | How long does a repair typically take? |
| **MTBF** (Mean Time Between Failures) | How long does equipment typically run between failures? |

**RPO drives backup frequency**; **RTO drives recovery architecture**. An RPO of one hour means backing up at least hourly. An RTO of fifteen minutes rules out restoring from tape and demands a warm or hot standby.

**MTBF is a reliability statistic** — higher is better, and it is what vendor datasheets quote. **MTTR is a repair statistic** — lower is better. They answer different questions and the exam contrasts them.

### Recovery sites

| Site type | Equipment | Data | Time to activate | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cold** | Space and power only | None | Days to weeks | Lowest |
| **Warm** | Hardware in place | Periodically synced | Hours | Moderate |
| **Hot** | Fully equipped and running | Continuously replicated | Minutes | Highest |

Match the site to the RTO. A cold site cannot serve a four-hour RTO no matter how well documented it is.

### Testing

A plan that has never been tested is a hypothesis. The named methods:

- **Tabletop exercise** — the team walks through the plan on paper. Cheap, catches gaps in process and contact details, proves nothing technically.
- **Validation test** — actually exercising the failover to confirm it works.

### Organisational documents

| Document | What it defines |
|---|---|
| **SLA** | Measurable service commitments — uptime percentage, response and resolution times |
| **MOU** | A general, often non-binding statement of intent between parties |
| **NDA** | Confidentiality of shared information |
| **AUP** | What users may and may not do with the network |

When a question asks which document to cite for a **specific, measurable** uptime or response guarantee, it is always the **SLA** — that measurability is exactly what separates it from an MOU.

### Documentation that supports operations

The objectives name a specific set, and questions ask which one to consult:

- **Physical versus logical diagrams** — how things are cabled versus how traffic flows.
- **Rack diagrams** — device positions by rack unit.
- **Cable maps** — which jack terminates to which patch panel port.
- **Layer 1, 2, and 3 diagrams** — physical, switching, and routing views.
- **Asset inventory** — hardware, software, licensing, warranty status.
- **IPAM** — IP address management, tracking what is assigned where.
- **Wireless survey and heat map** — coverage and signal strength by location.

### Lifecycle and configuration management

**EOL** means the vendor stops selling and developing the product. **EOS** means it stops receiving patches and support — and **EOS is the date that matters for security**, because a device can keep running for years past it while accumulating unpatched vulnerabilities.

**Configuration management** distinguishes the **production** configuration currently running, the **backup** configuration held for restoration, and the **baseline or golden** configuration representing known-good. Comparing production against baseline is how **configuration drift** is detected.

> Exam habit: RPO is about data loss and drives backup frequency. RTO is about downtime and drives architecture. Reading which one a scenario constrains tells you which solution it wants.

title: Network services, extra monitoring tools, and lifecycle management
summary: SLAAC, PTP, and NTS as services; port mirroring and API integration for monitoring; MTBF; and the EOL/EOS lifecycle.
body:
## Network services, and the operational vocabulary around them

The services that make a network usable, plus the lifecycle and management terms the objectives name.

### DHCP in detail

The lease exchange is **DORA**: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. The configuration concepts:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Scope** | The pool of addresses available for a subnet |
| **Reservation** | A specific address always issued to a specific MAC |
| **Exclusion** | Addresses within the scope the server must not hand out |
| **Lease time** | How long a client may keep an address before renewing |
| **Options** | Extra settings delivered with the lease — gateway, DNS, NTP, TFTP server |
| **Relay / IP helper** | Forwards DHCP broadcasts across a router to a server on another subnet |

The **relay** matters because DHCP Discover is a broadcast, and routers do not forward broadcasts. A client on a subnet with no local DHCP server gets nothing unless the router is configured with an **IP helper** address pointing at the server. "Clients on one VLAN get addresses, clients on another get APIPA" is very often a missing helper.

**Reservations** are the right answer for printers, access points, and appliances: the device stays on DHCP so it is centrally managed, but its address never changes.

### SLAAC and IPv6 addressing

**SLAAC** (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) lets an IPv6 host build its own address from a router advertisement, with no DHCP server involved at all. This is a genuine architectural difference from IPv4, where DHCP is effectively mandatory.

IPv6 transition mechanisms the objectives name:

- **Dual stack** — running IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously. The most common approach.
- **Tunneling** — carrying IPv6 traffic across an IPv4-only path.
- **NAT64** — translating between IPv6-only clients and IPv4-only servers.

### Time protocols

- **NTP** — the standard, accurate to milliseconds. Good enough for logs, authentication, and certificates.
- **PTP** — Precision Time Protocol, accurate to microseconds, for financial trading and industrial or telecom equipment where NTP is not tight enough.
- **NTS** — Network Time Security, adding authentication and integrity so a device cannot be tricked into accepting a spoofed time source.

Accurate time is not cosmetic: Kerberos rejects tickets when clocks drift, certificates appear invalid, and correlating logs across devices becomes impossible.

### Network access and management methods

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Site-to-site VPN** | Permanently joins two networks; users are unaware |
| **Client-to-site VPN** | An individual device connects into the network |
| **Clientless VPN** | Browser-based access with no VPN client installed |
| **Split tunnel** | Only corporate traffic goes through the tunnel |
| **Full tunnel** | All traffic goes through, allowing inspection |
| **Jump box / host** | A hardened intermediate system used to reach sensitive segments |
| **Console** | Direct physical serial access to a device |

**In-band versus out-of-band management** is an important distinction. In-band management shares the production network — convenient, but useless when the network is down, which is exactly when you need access. **Out-of-band** management uses a separate path (a console server, a cellular modem, a dedicated management network), so a device can be reached even when its production interfaces are unreachable. That is its entire value.

### Lifecycle management

- **EOL** — the vendor stops selling and developing the product.
- **EOS** — the vendor stops issuing patches and support. **This is the security-relevant date**: a device can keep running for years past EOS while accumulating unpatched vulnerabilities.
- **Decommissioning** — retiring hardware properly: wiping configuration and data, updating documentation and the asset inventory, and disposing of it responsibly.

**Software management** covers patches and bug fixes, operating system updates, and **firmware** — which is frequently neglected on network hardware precisely because it is not visible day to day.

### Change and configuration management

**Change management** requires a documented request, risk and impact analysis, approval, a scheduled window, a rollback plan, and post-change documentation.

**Configuration management** distinguishes three things:

- The **production configuration** currently running.
- The **backup configuration** held so a device can be restored or replaced quickly.
- The **baseline or golden configuration** representing known-good, against which drift is measured.

**Configuration drift** is what happens when devices are changed ad hoc and no longer match the baseline. Detecting it is a named monitoring capability.

> Exam habit: "clients on one subnet get addresses and clients on another do not" is a DHCP relay / IP helper question. Broadcasts do not cross routers, and that is the whole explanation.

title: Common network attacks, matched to their mechanism
summary: ARP spoofing, rogue DHCP, and evil twins — what each one actually does.
body:
## Network attacks, matched to their mechanism

Almost every attack in this objective works by **impersonating something trusted** or by **exhausting something finite**. Sorting them that way makes the list far easier to hold.

### Impersonation attacks

| Attack | What it impersonates |
|---|---|
| **ARP spoofing / poisoning** | The gateway's MAC address, on the local segment |
| **Rogue DHCP server** | The legitimate DHCP server |
| **Evil twin** | A legitimate wireless SSID |
| **DNS poisoning / spoofing** | A legitimate DNS answer |
| **Rogue access point** | An authorised AP on the corporate network |
| **On-path attack** | Both ends of a conversation, to each other |

**ARP spoofing** exploits the fact that ARP has no authentication. The attacker sends unsolicited replies claiming the gateway's IP belongs to their MAC, and traffic destined for the gateway comes to them instead. Result: a Layer 2 on-path position. Mitigations are dynamic ARP inspection and DHCP snooping on managed switches.

**A rogue DHCP server** hands out its own address as the gateway or DNS server, silently redirecting clients. It is often accidental — someone plugs a home router into the office network — which is exactly why DHCP snooping exists, permitting DHCP replies only from designated ports.

**An evil twin** broadcasts a familiar SSID so clients associate with it. Because many devices reconnect to remembered networks automatically, it frequently needs no user action at all.

### Exhaustion and disruption attacks

**DoS and DDoS** overwhelm a target so legitimate users cannot be served. The distributed form uses many compromised hosts at once, which makes simple source blocking ineffective. Two variants get named:

- **Reflected** — the attacker spoofs the victim's source address so third-party servers send their replies to the victim.
- **Amplified** — the same trick, choosing a protocol where the reply is far larger than the request, multiplying the attacker's bandwidth.

**MAC flooding** overwhelms a switch's CAM table with fabricated addresses. Once full, some switches fail open and flood all traffic out every port like a hub, letting an attacker on any port see traffic never meant for them. **Port security**, limiting MAC addresses per port, is the mitigation.

**VLAN hopping** reaches a VLAN the attacker should not have access to, either by negotiating a trunk (mitigated by disabling automatic trunk negotiation on access ports) or by **double tagging** (mitigated by not using the default VLAN as the native VLAN).

### Attacks against people

Social engineering bypasses technical controls entirely by targeting the operator:

- **Phishing** — fraudulent email harvesting credentials or delivering malware.
- **Dumpster diving** — recovering sensitive information from discarded material.
- **Shoulder surfing** — observing a screen or keypad directly.
- **Tailgating / piggybacking** — following an authorised person through a controlled door.

The mitigation for all four is **training and physical policy**, not firewalls — which is precisely the point the exam makes with them.

### Malware on the network

The exam covers malware lightly here: viruses, worms, ransomware, and trojans, with the network-relevant observation that **worms self-propagate** and therefore spread fastest across flat, unsegmented networks. Segmentation limits the blast radius.

### Spotting the pattern in a question

When a scenario describes an attack, ask what was faked or what was exhausted:

| Clue in the scenario | Attack |
|---|---|
| Traffic silently routing through an unexpected host on the LAN | ARP spoofing |
| Clients receiving wrong gateway or DNS settings | Rogue DHCP |
| Users connected to a familiar-looking Wi-Fi that is not yours | Evil twin |
| A correct hostname resolving to a hostile address | DNS poisoning |
| A switch suddenly flooding traffic to every port | MAC flooding |
| Traffic appearing on a VLAN it should not reach | VLAN hopping |
| Service unavailable under overwhelming traffic volume | DoS / DDoS |

> Exam habit: identify what the attacker is pretending to be. Gateway means ARP spoofing, DHCP server means rogue DHCP, SSID means evil twin, DNS answer means poisoning. Naming the impersonated thing names the attack.

title: 802.1X, RADIUS, and the screened subnet
summary: Port-based authentication and where to put a server the internet needs to reach.
body:
## Access control: 802.1X, NAC, and the screened subnet

Keeping unauthorised devices and users off the network, and containing what must be exposed.

### 802.1X port-based authentication

**802.1X** keeps a switch port closed until the connecting device authenticates. Plug in an unknown laptop and the port passes no traffic beyond the authentication exchange.

Three roles are involved:

- **Supplicant** — the client requesting access.
- **Authenticator** — the switch or access point controlling the port.
- **Authentication server** — usually **RADIUS**, which holds the credentials and makes the decision.

**EAP** is the framework carrying the actual authentication, with variants such as PEAP and EAP-TLS. EAP-TLS uses certificates on both sides and is the strongest common option.

### RADIUS versus TACACS+

| | RADIUS | TACACS+ |
|---|---|---|
| Transport | UDP | TCP |
| Encryption | Password only | The **entire payload** |
| AAA handling | Combines authentication and authorization | Separates all three |
| Typical use | Network **access** — 802.1X, VPN, Wi-Fi | **Administrative** access to network devices |

The practical split: RADIUS for getting users onto the network, TACACS+ for controlling what administrators may do on the devices themselves — its separation of authorization allows per-command control.

### NAC

**Network Access Control** goes beyond identity to **device posture**: is the operating system patched, is antivirus present and current, does it meet policy? Devices failing the check can be denied or placed in a **quarantine VLAN** with access only to remediation resources.

This matters most for **BYOD** and guest scenarios, where the organisation does not manage the endpoint.

### Other access controls

- **Port security** limits which, and how many, MAC addresses may use a switch port, and can shut the port down on violation.
- **MAC filtering** permits only listed addresses — weak, because MAC addresses are transmitted in the clear and easily cloned. Treat it as a speed bump.
- **Disabling unused ports** removes the easiest physical path onto the network and costs nothing.

### Zones and the screened subnet

Firewall design divides the network into zones of differing trust:

- **Trusted** — the internal LAN.
- **Untrusted** — the internet.
- **Screened subnet (DMZ)** — a semi-trusted zone in between.

A public-facing server belongs in the **screened subnet**, never on the internal LAN. Traffic from the internet reaches the screened subnet; traffic from the screened subnet **into** the internal network is tightly restricted. If the web server is compromised, the attacker has not landed among the workstations and file servers.

If a question asks where to place a public web server, that is the answer — and "on the internal VLAN with a firewall rule" is the distractor.

### Filtering and rules

- **ACLs** — ordered permit/deny rules matching source, destination, port, and protocol. Order matters: the first match wins, and a rule below a broader one may never be evaluated. Most implementations end with an **implicit deny**.
- **URL and content filtering** — blocking by address or category, typically at a proxy or firewall.
- **Key management** — the lifecycle around encryption keys: generation, secure storage, rotation, and revocation. Encryption is only as strong as the handling of its keys.

### Device hardening

The baseline the objectives name:

1. **Change default credentials** — published for every model and the first thing tried.
2. **Disable unused ports and services**, including WAN-side remote administration.
3. **Keep firmware updated.**
4. **Use secure management protocols** — SSH rather than Telnet, HTTPS rather than HTTP, SNMPv3 rather than v2c.
5. **Restrict management access** to a dedicated network or specific addresses.

> Exam habit: 802.1X authenticates the **device or user** before the port opens; NAC additionally assesses the device's **security posture**. If a scenario mentions checking patch level or antivirus status before granting access, it wants NAC.

title: Security fundamentals: the CIA triad, risk vocabulary, and identity systems
summary: Confidentiality/integrity/availability, risk vs vulnerability vs threat, and how PKI/IAM/SSO/SAML fit together.
body:
## Security fundamentals: the vocabulary underneath every question

Domain 4 leans heavily on precise terminology. These words are not interchangeable, and the exam relies on that.

### The CIA triad

Every control exists to protect one of three properties:

- **Confidentiality** — only authorised parties can read the data. Encryption, access control.
- **Integrity** — data has not been altered, and you would know if it had. Hashing, digital signatures.
- **Availability** — authorised parties can reach the data or service when needed. Redundancy, DDoS mitigation, backups.

The distinction the exam presses: **ransomware that encrypts files without stealing them is primarily an availability failure**, not confidentiality. Nothing was read; it is simply no longer accessible.

**Non-repudiation** is the frequently forgotten fourth property: the sender cannot credibly deny having sent something. Digital signatures provide it, because only the holder of the private key could have produced the signature.

### Risk terminology

Four words that are not synonyms:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Threat** | Something that could cause harm — an attacker, a storm, an insider |
| **Vulnerability** | A weakness a threat could exploit — an unpatched server, a weak policy |
| **Exploit** | The actual method or code that takes advantage of the vulnerability |
| **Risk** | The likelihood and impact of a threat successfully exploiting a vulnerability |

You cannot eliminate threats; you reduce vulnerabilities, which lowers risk.

### Encryption, by data state

- **Data in transit** — moving across a network. Protected by TLS, IPsec, VPN.
- **Data at rest** — stored on disk. Protected by full-disk or database encryption.

A stolen server drive read directly is an **at-rest** problem; traffic sniffed on the wire is an **in-transit** problem. They call for different controls, and the exam expects the matching one.

### Certificates and PKI

**PKI** is the system of certificate authorities, certificates, and key pairs that makes TLS trustworthy. A **CA** vouches that a public key genuinely belongs to the named entity.

A **self-signed certificate** is signed by its own key rather than a trusted CA. It provides the same **encryption** as a CA-signed certificate but no third-party **identity verification**, which is why browsers warn on it. Acceptable internally where the certificate is deliberately trusted; not acceptable for a public service.

### Identity and access management

**IAM** is the umbrella: creating, managing, and revoking identities and their access.

**Authentication** methods and protocols:

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **MFA** | Two or more factors from **different** categories |
| **SSO** | Authenticate once, reach multiple systems |
| **SAML** | The protocol carrying an authentication assertion between systems — how SSO is delivered |
| **RADIUS** | AAA for network access — 802.1X, VPN, Wi-Fi |
| **TACACS+** | AAA for device administration; encrypts the whole payload and separates authorization |
| **LDAP / LDAPS** | Directory queries; LDAPS wraps them in TLS |
| **Time-based authentication** | Restricting access to permitted hours |

**SSO is the user experience; SAML is the mechanism.** That is the distinction the exam draws.

**Authorization** concepts:

- **Least privilege** — exactly the access the role requires, nothing more.
- **Role-based access control** — permissions attached to job functions rather than individuals, so access changes by reassigning a role.

**Geofencing** restricts access by geographic location, adding a location condition on top of normal authentication.

### Physical security and deception

Physical controls — **cameras** and **locks** — matter because an attacker with physical access bypasses most software controls.

**Deception technologies** are deliberately attractive decoys:

- **Honeypot** — a single decoy system, made to look valuable, deployed to attract and study attackers away from real assets.
- **Honeynet** — an entire decoy network of them, for observing multi-step attacker behaviour.

Their value is high-fidelity alerting: nobody has a legitimate reason to touch them, so any interaction is meaningful.

### Compliance and data locality

- **PCI DSS** — mandatory for any organisation handling payment card data, regardless of size.
- **GDPR** — the EU regulation covering EU residents' personal data, wherever the organisation is based.
- **Data locality** — legal or contractual requirements that data physically remain in a given country or region. A cloud deployment storing EU customer data only in the US can violate locality even with flawless encryption and access control, because *where* the data lives is itself the requirement.

### Segmentation as the universal answer

**IoT and IIoT**, **SCADA/ICS/OT**, **guest** networks, and **BYOD** devices all get the same treatment: put them on their own segment, isolated from the corporate network. They frequently cannot be patched, run outdated software, or are not managed by the organisation at all. Isolation is the compensating control, and it is the expected answer whenever a scenario describes equipment that cannot be secured directly.

> Exam habit: "unpatched server" is the vulnerability, "a known attacker group" is the threat, "the code that abuses the flaw" is the exploit, and "how likely this is and what it costs" is the risk. Questions test the boundaries between these four constantly.

title: Compliance, segmentation, and the rest of the attack surface
summary: PCI DSS/GDPR, OT/ICS/SCADA segmentation, honeypots, and the social-engineering and filtering basics.
body:
## Applying security: hardening, filtering, and the human layer

Domain 4's practical half — what you actually configure, and the attacks that target people rather than protocols.

### Device hardening

The baseline, roughly in order of value:

1. **Change default credentials.** Default usernames and passwords for every model are published and searchable. This is the single most exploited weakness in network equipment.
2. **Disable unused ports and services.** Every enabled service is attack surface; every live port is a physical path in.
3. **Keep firmware patched.** Network device firmware is easy to forget precisely because it is invisible day to day.
4. **Use secure management protocols** — SSH not Telnet, HTTPS not HTTP, SNMPv3 not v2c.
5. **Restrict management access** to a dedicated management network or specific source addresses, and never expose it to the internet.

### Network access control

- **802.1X** — port-based authentication; the port stays closed until the device authenticates against RADIUS.
- **Port security** — limits how many, and which, MAC addresses may use a port, optionally shutting it down on violation.
- **MAC filtering** — permits only listed addresses. Weak, because MAC addresses travel in the clear and are trivially cloned. A speed bump, not a control.
- **NAC posture assessment** — checks patch level, antivirus state, and configuration before granting access, quarantining non-compliant devices.

### Security rules and filtering

**ACLs** are ordered permit/deny rules matching source, destination, port, and protocol. Two properties matter:

- **Order is significant.** The first matching rule wins, so a broad rule placed above a specific one makes the specific one unreachable.
- Most implementations end with an **implicit deny** — anything not explicitly permitted is dropped.

**URL filtering** blocks specific addresses; **content filtering** blocks by category. Both typically sit at a proxy or firewall.

### Zones

- **Trusted** — the internal network.
- **Untrusted** — the internet.
- **Screened subnet (DMZ)** — the semi-trusted zone between them, where internet-facing services live.

A public web server belongs in the screened subnet so that compromising it does not put the attacker on the internal LAN. Traffic from the screened subnet *into* the internal network is tightly restricted — that restriction is the entire point of the design.

### Key management

Encryption is only as strong as the handling of its keys. The lifecycle covers **generation**, **secure storage** (often in an HSM), **distribution**, **rotation** on a schedule, and **revocation** when a key is compromised or a person leaves. A perfectly implemented cipher with a key stored in a text file on a shared drive protects nothing.

### Social engineering

These attacks bypass every technical control by targeting the operator:

| Technique | Method |
|---|---|
| **Phishing** | Fraudulent email harvesting credentials or delivering malware |
| **Dumpster diving** | Recovering sensitive information from discarded material |
| **Shoulder surfing** | Observing a screen or keypad directly |
| **Tailgating / piggybacking** | Following an authorised person through a controlled door |

The mitigation is **training and physical policy**, not firewalls — and that is exactly why the objectives include them. A well-configured network is still compromised by someone who holds the door open.

### Operational technology segmentation

Industrial and embedded environments come with their own vocabulary:

- **ICS** — Industrial Control Systems, the umbrella for systems controlling physical processes.
- **SCADA** — a type of ICS for large-scale, geographically distributed control such as utilities and pipelines.
- **OT** — Operational Technology, hardware and software directly monitoring or controlling physical devices, as distinct from IT, which handles data.
- **IIoT** — industrial IoT devices in manufacturing settings.

All four receive the same answer: **segment them from the corporate network**. They often run unpatchable software on long hardware lifecycles and were designed for availability and safety rather than security.

**Guest** and **BYOD** networks get the same treatment for a different reason: the organisation does not control those endpoints.

### Compliance recap

**PCI DSS** for cardholder data, **GDPR** for EU personal data, and **data locality** requirements about where data physically resides. Recognising that a scenario has triggered one of these is usually the point of the question.

> Exam habit: when a scenario describes equipment that cannot be patched — industrial controllers, medical devices, legacy systems, IoT — the expected answer is network segmentation. It is the compensating control for "we cannot fix the device itself."

title: The troubleshooting methodology, and why order matters
summary: The six official steps, and the one the exam most likes to test.
body:
## The troubleshooting methodology, and why the order matters

CompTIA's sequence appears on every exam in the family, and Network+ tests the order more than the wording.

### The steps

1. **Identify the problem** — gather information, question users, identify symptoms, determine what changed, duplicate the problem if possible, and approach multiple problems individually.
2. **Establish a theory of probable cause** — question the obvious, and consider multiple approaches.
3. **Test the theory to determine the cause** — if confirmed, determine next steps; if not, establish a new theory **or escalate**.
4. **Establish a plan of action** to resolve the problem and identify potential effects.
5. **Implement the solution or escalate** as necessary.
6. **Verify full system functionality** and, if applicable, implement preventive measures.
7. **Document** findings, actions, outcomes, and lessons learned.

### The step most often tested

Questions routinely describe a technician who has formed a theory and ask what comes **next**. The trap answer is implementing the fix. The correct answer is **testing the theory first**.

An untested theory is a guess, and acting on guesses is how you replace three components without fixing anything. The step even names its own fork: theory confirmed, proceed; theory not confirmed, form a new one or escalate.

### "Determine if anything has changed"

This sub-step of identifying the problem carries more weight than its length suggests. Most things that break were working until something changed — a configuration edit, a patch, a new device, a storm overnight. Asking what changed frequently produces the answer before any testing begins.

### Two named approaches

- **Top-to-bottom or bottom-to-top through the OSI model.** Bottom-up is usually more efficient, because a Layer 1 fault explains every failure above it. Confirm the link before theorising about DNS.
- **Divide and conquer.** Test at the middle of the path; whichever half proves faulty gets divided again. Efficient when you already have a sense of where the fault sits.

### Identify potential effects

Step 4 explicitly includes identifying what else the fix might affect. Rebooting a core switch to clear a fault also drops every device behind it. On a production network that means a maintenance window and notification, not an immediate reboot — and the exam does test that judgement.

### Verify, then document

**Verification** means the whole system, not just the original symptom. Replacing a switch restores connectivity — but did the VLANs come back? Do the phones still get their voice VLAN? Preventive measures belong here too: if a dust-blocked fan caused the overheat, cleaning it now prevents the repeat.

**Documentation is last and it is not optional.** "Lessons learned" is explicitly part of it. Its value is to whoever meets the same fault next, including you.

### Why each step exists

| Skipping | Produces |
|---|---|
| Identify the problem | Fixing something that was not broken |
| Establish a theory | Random component swapping |
| **Test the theory** | Expensive guessing |
| Plan of action | Collateral damage from an unplanned change |
| Verify functionality | A second ticket for what you broke |
| Document | The same diagnosis repeated indefinitely |

### Escalation is legitimate

Both step 3 and step 5 name escalation as a valid outcome. Recognising that a problem is beyond your access, expertise, or authority is part of the process, not a failure of it — and on a question where the technician clearly lacks the necessary access, escalation is the right answer.

> Exam habit: locate exactly where the described technician is in the sequence, then give the very next step. Do not jump to the fix, and do not skip verification on the way to documentation.

title: Cable faults and the tools that diagnose them
summary: Split pairs, opens, shorts, and the tester that finds each.
body:
## Cable faults, interface counters, and the tools that find them

Physical-layer problems have precise names, and each has a tool that identifies it.

### Cable faults

| Fault | What it is | Symptom |
|---|---|---|
| **Open** | A broken conductor | No continuity; link never comes up |
| **Short** | Two conductors touching | Near-zero resistance where there should be none |
| **Split pair** | Wires from different pairs used as one pair | Link may come up; badly degraded at speed |
| **TX/RX reversed** | Transmit and receive swapped | No link despite a physical connection |
| **Attenuation** | Signal loss over distance | Fails beyond the maximum run length |
| **Crosstalk** | Signal bleed between adjacent pairs | Errors and retransmissions |

**Split pair** is the fault worth dwelling on, because it is counterintuitive. All eight conductors are continuous, so a simple continuity check passes and the link may even come up. But the pairs are no longer twisted together as designed, so the noise cancellation that twisting provides is gone and crosstalk destroys performance at gigabit speeds. Only a proper wiremap tester catches it.

**Attenuation** is why the 100 metre limit exists for twisted-pair Ethernet. A 130 metre run may appear to work and then fail intermittently, which looks like a mysterious fault rather than a distance problem.

### Choosing the right cable

- **Single-mode versus multimode fiber** — single-mode for long distances, multimode for shorter runs within a building. Mixing them, or mismatching transceivers, breaks the link.
- **Category 5e / 6 / 6a / 8** — must match the required speed **and** distance. Cat 6 does 10 Gbps only to about 55 m; Cat 6a carries it the full 100 m.
- **STP versus UTP** — shielded cable helps in high-interference environments but must be properly grounded to work as intended.
- **Plenum versus non-plenum** — plenum-rated jacketing is required by fire code in air-handling spaces.

### Interface counters

Switch port counters name the fault directly:

| Counter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **CRC errors** | Frames arriving corrupted — bad termination, damaged cable, interference |
| **Runts** | Frames below the 64-byte minimum — collisions or duplex mismatch |
| **Giants** | Frames above the MTU — MTU mismatch |
| **Drops** | Frames discarded, typically congestion or buffer exhaustion |

**Rising CRC errors on a recently re-terminated cable** point squarely at the termination. That is a favourite exam pairing.

### Port status

- **Error disabled (err-disabled)** — the switch protectively shut the port down after a violation, commonly **port security** (an unexpected MAC) or **BPDU guard** (a switch plugged into an access port). Identify the trigger before re-enabling; blindly re-enabling recreates it.
- **Administratively down** — someone disabled it deliberately.
- **Suspended** — typically a channel/aggregation mismatch.

### Duplex and speed mismatch

A classic slow-network fault: one end fixed at full duplex, the other auto-negotiating and falling back to half. The link comes up and works, but throughput collapses under load and late collisions accumulate. The fix is to set both ends consistently — ideally both to auto-negotiate.

### PoE problems

Power over Ethernet failures come from a **power budget exceeded** on the switch, an **incorrect standard** (a device needing 802.3at offered only 802.3af power), or a faulty cable or port. If most devices work and one does not, suspect that device's requirement or its physical path rather than a switch-wide budget.

### Transceiver problems

A **mismatch** — wrong wavelength, wrong mode, wrong speed — or inadequate **signal strength** produces a link that will not come up or that errors heavily. Fiber transceivers must match at both ends.

### The tools

| Tool | Finds |
|---|---|
| **Cable tester (wiremap)** | Opens, shorts, miswires, split pairs |
| **TDR / OTDR** | The **distance** to a break, for copper and fiber respectively |
| **Tone generator and probe** | Which physical cable is which |
| **Loopback plug** | Whether a port's own transmit/receive circuitry works |
| **Visual fault locator** | Fiber breaks and tight bends, by injecting visible light |
| **Multimeter** | Voltage and continuity on copper |
| **Wi-Fi analyser** | Channel usage, signal strength, interference |
| **Network tap** | A passive copy of traffic on a link |

Note the copper/fiber split: toners and multimeters are copper tools, since fiber carries light rather than current. OTDRs and visual fault locators are the fiber equivalents.

> Exam habit: "where is the break?" is a TDR or OTDR. "Which cable is this?" is a toner and probe. "Is this cable wired correctly?" is a wiremap tester. The verb in the question picks the tool.
